segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan.
Today, a warning about testosterone supplements in men.
A discovery in the lab which could increase the success rates of organ transplantation.
Should doctors be allowed to refuse care to patients because they object to the treatment, the doctors that is, on moral or religious grounds?
A leading ethicist says no.
And a paradox which emerged yesterday in an Australian study published in the prestigious New England Journal of Medicine.
Obstructive sleep apnea, usually where people snore badly and then stop breathing for a few seconds at a time,
is linked to a high risk of heart disease.
So much so that some manufacturers of so-called CPAP machines,
where positive air pressure through the nose keeps the airways open,
have suggested that the machines reduce the chances of a heart attack or stroke.
Now an Australian trial suggests that ain't so.
With me is one of the authors, sleep specialist and researcher Professor Ron Grinstein.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Good evening, Norman.
What is the link between sleep apnea and heart disease?
Well, look, I think there's quite strong and compelling evidence
that patients with sleep apnea as a group have higher rates
of cardiovascular disease and cerebrovascular disease.
Cerebrovascular meaning stroke.
Yeah, so it's an association.
But they also share a lot of the risk factors that people
who get those heart and brain disorders have,
which is that they are obese
and they have sort of vascular risk factors.
So the issue of whether treatment of sleep apnea
could potentially reduce the risk
of these events happening in people
has always been a challenge to the field.
Which takes it from an association to cause and effect.
Exactly.
So rather than just sitting side by side,
tell me where you did this trial.
sorry tell me what you did in this trial right well um the trial so when i think about it started
about 11 years ago and it started really as a conversation by people who were uh in australia
who were working in this field we thought we needed to do this study and my colleague and we
have to say to begin with that the the the the ancestors of your group actually invented cpap
worldwide i mean that's where the idea came from yeah it's an australian invention
um so my colleague Doug McEvoy who at Flinders University and Craig Anderson is the George
Institute in Sydney um really drove this study um and we set up um an executive group to look at
um how to design such a study and basically we ended up uh recruiting about 2,700 or randomizing
2,700 patients into two groups. One who received this continuous positive airway pressure plus
usual care versus another group who were randomized to usual care alone. Importantly,
the patients that we chose all had pre-existing vascular events. They'd had a heart attack
or they had angina with proven cardiovascular disease.
So a high risk of another event.
Yeah, because of high risk, because we were looking for a higher return in terms of event rates.
So what did you find?
Well, the primary finding was that after an average of 3.7 years follow-up, there was no
difference in outcomes between the group that received the CPAP therapy in usual care versus
the usual care alone. So there was no advantage of giving people CPAP if the aim of the exercise was
to reduce cardiovascular events and strokes.
What we also found was there was a benefit in reducing symptoms,
sleepiness and impaired wellbeing.
These got better.
But the primary endpoint, primary variable of interest was not achieved.
What does that tell you?
I mean, about CPAP?
I mean, does this mean that ResMed needs to put out a profit warning?
I mean, we shouldn't pick out one in particular,
but essentially do the manufacturers have to change their marketing now?
Oh, look, I think it's, you know, if you permit me to focus on what doctors should do.
Okay.
All right.
This is a way from tiger country.
All right, Professor Gresti.
I think as people working in this area,
I think we really have to interpret the evidence for our patients,
which is that if you, and I actually saw a patient today
who just happens to be a semi-retired cardiologist
who's got very few symptoms of sleep apnea,
but he's got sleep apnea
and he's previously had coronary bypass surgery.
And the question was...
So a cardiologist who walks the talk, clearly.
Yeah, and he kind of, you know,
so what do I do for this gentleman?
And basically, you know,
I'm just purely on the basis
of trying to improve his cardiovascular prognosis.
So I don't think I've got, you know,
the evidence from this study to justify that. However, you know, he may well have symptoms
which, you know, may warrant treatment. So you don't really want to treat this.
You don't want to tell patients, look, I'm going to give you this CPAP, even though you feel
perfectly well, we're going to give you a CPAP machine because it's going to reduce your risk
or your future risk of recurrence of heart disease or stroke.
So it's just for the sleep apnea itself. And just briefly in a minute or two that we've got left,
Where does continuous positive airways pressure sit amongst weight loss, surgical devices, things that you stick in your mouth, you know, splints and so on in terms of benefits?
I mean, we seem to be rolling the dice totally on CPAP machines.
Yeah.
I mean, to paraphrase one of our politicians, we live in exciting times.
And the treatment choices are widening.
We've studied extensively dental devices for sleep apnea,
which seem to work reasonably well when compared to CPAP.
So are these like mouth guards?
Yeah, they're sort of splints that basically you've got to make them individually for the patient.
And they essentially move the bottom or the mandible, the bottom jaw forward,
creating space behind the tongue.
And these are reasonably effective treatments when compared to CPAP.
What about bariatric surgery?
Does that relieve snoring?
And sleep apnea?
Yeah, I think bariatric surgery in people where there is, you know, other health issues
as well as a sleep apnea probably justified.
And we've had quite good success because most of our patients are male.
We've had very good success with just, you know, diet, exercise and sustaining those
effects for at least a year and getting reduction in sleep apnea.
Ron, thanks very much for joining us.
No problem, Ron.
Ron Grinstein is Chief Investigator of the NHMRC Centre for Translational Sleep and Circadian Neurobiology at the Wilcock Institute of Medical Research at the University of Sydney.
You're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio in Canada.
I'm Norman Swan and we have links to the references for all our stories.
If you want the references, you can go to our website at ABC Radio National.
Guidelines for doctors treating men with what's called hypogonadism have been released by the Endocrine Society of Australia in today's edition of the Medical Journal of Australia.
And they contain a warning about the use of testosterone supplements.
One of the leaders of the group was Professor Boo Yap of the University of Western Australia School of Medicine and Pharmacology.
And he's in our Perth studio. Welcome, Boo, to The Health Report.
Thank you.
Just tell us what hypogonadism is.
So hypergonadism is a medical condition where you have a problem with the pituitary gland or the testes
and you're unable to make enough testosterone for yourself.
So your testosterone levels are low and it's associated with a range of symptoms and signs.
Such as?
You may feel your libido is low, so you've lost interest in sex, or you may feel tired or lethargic.
Some men may notice that they seem to be gaining fat, losing a bit of muscle.
So it may actually present with reduced bone mass is another example.
So there are quite a few different symptoms and signs.
So this isn't the male menopause.
The reason for the loss of testosterone is something else.
Yes.
So we are talking about men who have medical conditions affecting the hypothalamus or the pituitary gland or the testes
who cannot make enough testosterone for themselves.
And just to explain, the testes, just like the ovaries,
are driven by the brain, hormones from the brain
that send signals to the testes to produce testosterone.
Yes.
And so somewhere along that pathway, things can go wrong.
Yes.
And you've told us how you have it.
And is testosterone the only treatment?
Well, there are two separate components.
So obviously one function of the testes is to make testosterone.
The other one is to make sperm.
So if you want fertility and you have this kind of problem,
then it's a very different approach.
So if you actually want fertility,
then testosterone is actually, we may make things a bit worse.
So you have to sort that out first and then testosterone will treat symptoms and signs.
So this can turn up in an IVF clinic with a couple who are infertile
and it turns out that it's the man's issue and it could be hypogonadism
and then you've got to work out how you're going to treat it.
Yes, that's one of the possible ways it could present, yes.
And for other men where infertility is not the issue,
then what you're doing is testosterone replacement.
Yes.
And testosterone is the best hormone
and there are different formulations
so we can actually individualize treatment
and find a formulation that suits a particular man.
What do you mean by different formulations?
You can give testosterone as an intramuscular injection
or you can give it as a gel or a cream or a liquid, so transdermally.
So, you know, there are different options and it depends on a particular man's preference.
And before we get on to just your recommendations, there's one more thing I just wanted to ask you,
which is how you make the diagnosis of hypergolinism apart from the story?
Because, you know, you don't want to say this is just hypergolinism without knowing for sure.
Sure. Well, the symptoms and signs are really important.
The examination may be quite helpful.
and then obviously you do a blood test
and you can measure testosterone in the blood as well.
And the hormones from the brain as well, do they go up?
Yes, so we measure luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone, LH and FSH
and if you have a testicular problem, they go up
whereas if you have a problem in the pituitary gland, they tend to be low or normal.
So there's ways of diagnosing this.
Now what's the issue with prescribing testosterone
testosterone that you were warning about in this guideline in today's Medical Journal of Australia?
Sure. I think the guidelines, I mean, the most important point is that we have recommended that
testosterone be given to men who have pathological hypergonadism. They have a problem in the
pituitary or in the testes. Now, there are a lot of other conditions where your testosterone may be
low and this includes men who are older or men who have medical problems or men who may be taking
medications such as glucocorticoids or opioids. So steroids or morphine like drugs. Yes. So in
those men, testosterone levels may be low, but we don't have enough evidence to justify giving
them testosterone or at least not as yet. Right. Now you're worried about heart disease.
Yes, there is a risk of adverse events, cardiovascular adverse events,
and it seems to be in those men who are older or frail and have already got heart disease.
When you mean cardiovascular events, that's what I was talking to Ron Grunstein a moment about.
So, you're talking about heart attacks and strokes.
Heart attacks and strokes, yes.
So, it might be that older men, frail men, and men who have already got cardiovascular disease,
that we might just have to be a little bit cautious in those men.
What does that mean for a general practitioner or a specialist in this area?
So if those men have pathological hypogonadism,
they should still be considered for treatment,
but you might want to initiate treatment a little bit more slowly
or start at a lower dose and monitor more carefully.
Obviously, first, you want to make sure that whatever their existing heart disease is,
that it's already under treatment.
For men who do not have pathological hypergonadism,
well, we would probably advise against giving them testosterone,
particularly in the setting where they may be at higher risk of adverse events.
So if a man's feeling fatigued and claims that he's suffering from the male menopause.
Okay. Oh, well, yes. Okay. We don't like that male menopause.
But there is an important...
One of them would take you to rise to the bait.
Well, there is an important caveat in all of this,
which is that for the men without pathological hypergonadism,
There are a lot of areas where we've recommended they shouldn't have testosterone,
but because there's not enough evidence.
So we do actually, this is an important area where we do need to do a lot more research.
Testosterone may have benefits, it may have risks,
but we need to do more research to clarify those.
But coming to the bottom line here, hypogonadism,
male hypogonadism is really just about the only indication for testosterone
at the moment on an evidence base.
Yep. If you look at the evidence, if you have male hypergonalism, then yes, you should be treated.
So yes, you could say that that's the case.
And all the other scenarios that we've mentioned, we really need to do more research to define what the benefits and the risks are.
And is there any such thing as the andropause?
The decline in testosterone as men grow older is actually very gradual.
So if you look at all the studies, our own included,
older men, even if they're very healthy,
will have a lower testosterone than younger men.
But there isn't the abrupt decline that you see in women
who go through the menopausal transition.
But Buye, I thought your longitudinal study in Western Australia
showed that you had 80-year-old men with the testosterone of younger men
because they were very fit, they had good musculature,
and that in fact it's not an inevitable part of aging
that you've got this group of men who are pretty testosterone-loaded.
There are two studies. The one that you referred to is a slightly different one from the one that we've done in Western Australia.
You can have older men who are really healthy and they have testosterone levels comparable to younger men.
But in our study, if you take a large group of really healthy 70 to 89-year-old men,
then their testosterone levels, the range that you see, is in fact lower than healthy 21 to 35-year-olds.
So there's the odd exception, but the average bears out.
Well, this is an area which is, you know, you could say there's ongoing debate over this area.
But yes, the reference range is low in really healthy older men,
but you can have very healthy older men with levels comparable to younger men.
Bu Yap, thank you for joining us on The Health Report.
No, not at all. Pleasure.
Professor Bu Yap from the University of Western Australia School of Medicine and Pharmacology.
And again, we'll have the references for that story.
if you're concerned about hypergonadism on the Health Report's website.
Researchers in Melbourne may have found a substance
which helps to protect organs such as kidneys
being donated for transplantation from a common cause of damage.
If it pans out, the result will be higher success rates
from these precious donations.
The substance is called folistatin,
and one of the research leaders was Professor David de Kretzer
of the Hudson Institute of Medical Research at Monash University,
and he's in our Melbourne studio.
Welcome to the Health Report, David.
Nice to be here.
What is the problem you're trying to solve here?
Well, basically, it transplants.
When you take an organ out in, say, Sydney,
and the donor that's matched for him is in Melbourne,
that transplant is off its blood supply for maybe 6, 10 hours.
And when you get reperfusion of blood,
you actually create an inflammatory response.
And the inflammatory response produces a substance called Activen,
which is actually a hormonal stimulation,
but is also the major controller of your body's inflammatory response.
So this is called a reperfusion injury?
Yes, a reperfusion injury is absolutely right, yes.
So basically, some studies that we've done
shows that if you put actually folistatin into the preservation solutions of organs,
that you can actually attenuate that damage and result in a better transplant.
and especially in lung transplants where you can get preservation of aeration of the air sacs,
but those air sacs may not be supplied with blood.
Therefore, it's sort of dead space, essentially.
So I know that St. Vincent's Hospital in Sydney has got this innovation called Heart in a Box
where they perfuse hearts and manage to get much greater success rates in terms of length of time.
Is this the sort of technology that you could add to to improve things?
Absolutely.
And is it all organs? Because you did this study in kidneys.
Yes, we haven't done the studies in kidneys.
We've done some different studies in kidneys in that, again,
basically if you interrupt the blood supply to the kidneys for a period of time,
you actually create an inflammatory response, active and levels rise.
And again, if you give the mouse folly statin
before you actually clamp the blood vessel to the kidney,
you can actually attenuate and decrease the damage.
So folistatin is a very powerful substance
which has the potential for multiple applications
associated with inflammation and tissue damage.
Well, that was going to be my next question.
So just the study that we've picked up on here
is actually the study of mice
where you've shown that it works on this substance called activin
to reduce the injury in kidneys in mice.
But if you are actually inhibiting inflammation,
you're messing with the immune system.
could you get adverse immune effects by this?
Look, that's one of the issues that also needs to be looked at more closely.
In an acute situation, basically blocking the inflammatory response is beneficial.
I mean, there's data in wounding studies to show that if you give folistatin,
you can actually decrease the degree of scar formation.
So, you know, there are multiple uses of this substance.
and it is going to be a very powerful modulator of inflammation.
Now, what happens in mice does not necessarily happen in humans.
What evidence have you got that this could work in human tissue?
Well, certainly the studies that I was describing in relationship to transplantation
and the rise in acrobin, those were done basically in blood samples
from patients who were undergoing lung transplantation, human lung transplantation.
So this is showing that, if you like, the activin levels rise in relationship to certain aspects of transplantation surgery, especially the ischemia.
Also, substances like heparin, also anticoagulants, can release activin from tissue stores.
Activin is bound to folly statins.
So it could make it worse.
Through a positive charge system, and heparin being negatively charged releases it.
So if I was to give you a single shot of heparin, you'd get a single pulse of activin and folly statin released.
If I gave you a square wave, you'd get a square wave.
So, you know, basically your tissues and surfaces of cells actually have a coating in their basement membranes of activin and folly statin there.
So you're trying to commercialize this.
I mean, how long before you think that you're able to do proper trials in humans and give it a go?
Well, we're now in a position, we've obviously gone from a test tube to 1,000-litre fermentation to produce folly statin for human use.
It's been tested in two animal species without any side effects.
It's been given initially to humans in the first instance.
And here again, one of the things that we have to do in trials is to show that the drug is actually effective.
Well, a normal subject is actually not inflamed.
So one actually has to create an inflammation in a normal subject, and we're delivering
folistatin for lung purposes using a nebulizer system.
So basically, there was no experience here in Australia doing that, so we were able to
do such a study in Manchester, where there's been previous studies like this done and showed
very clearly that giving folistatin in a nebulizer system actually decreased the number of white
blood cells that are in the sputum of men who've been exposed to lipopolysaccharide. So we've
proved efficacy in normal subjects. So you're on the runway. That's fascinating. Thank you very
much for joining us on The Health Report. It's a pleasure. Professor David de Kretzer of the
Hudson Institute of Medical Research at Monash University in Melbourne. A leading ethicist is
going to argue in a lecture in Queensland later this week that doctors and other health professionals
like pharmacists should not be allowed to deny patients access to care because they, the doctors
or pharmacists conscientiously object to it.
The commonest examples would be contraception
and termination of pregnancy, but there are others.
Professor Julian Savulesko joins me from our Brisbane studio.
Julian is Professor of Practical Ethics
at the University of Oxford.
Welcome to The Health Report, Julian.
Good evening.
Just give me your argument.
Roll it out.
Well, there are two main arguments.
By allowing a conscientious objection clause,
as Victorian legislation does,
you open the door to women being denied medical services. So one study in the United States
around 10 years ago reported 15% of doctors wouldn't inform people of procedures that were
legal and 30% wouldn't refer on to another practitioner. That means in the US about 100
million people are going to be denied some medical service they're entitled to.
Such as?
Well, such as contraception, abortion, sterilisation, and in those states where assisted suicide is legal assisted suicide.
The second main argument is really a moral one.
Why should the medical care that a patient gets depend on the personal values, often the religious values, of the doctor that they happen to attend?
There are principles of law and ethics that should govern how treatments are delivered to patients, and doctors should certainly have their own values.
but at the end of the day, the patient should be entitled to receive medical care that is legal,
that's in their interests and that they want. And do we know the extent of the problem in
Australia? Well, there's certainly evidence, you know... With the problem being, if you're right,
denial of access to care. Well, if you're in a country town where the only general practitioner
has a religious objection to contraception or abortion, you're going to be in trouble.
And often this causes delays so that what would have been early terminations of pregnancy become late terminations of pregnancy, where the fetus is then viable.
So particularly in large countries such as Canada and Australia, this has real implications for people that live in remote areas that are effectively denied care.
In some states of the United States, there's only one abortion clinic for a whole state because of this kind of phenomenon.
Well, that's not necessarily the conscientious objection. That's more of the political environment
of the state, isn't it? Well, it's people determining care on the basis of values rather
than on some legal and ethical principles. And I think you're going to see effectively
the same sorts of things in remote areas of Australia.
So does that mean that when you're doing an interview for a medical school,
if you're a member of Opus Dei, you don't get in or what?
Well, in my view, there's three ways to deal with it.
One is simply to not allow a legal right of conscientious objection,
and that's precisely what Sweden and Finland have done,
and they have excellent care for women,
and they haven't discouraged good people from taking up medicine.
And the other one is to screen people on entry to medical school.
So just give me that screening story again,
because you're surely not going to deny Catholics entry to medical,
highly religious believing Catholics to medical school.
Well, there's plenty of specialities in medicine that you can do that don't involve contraception,
abortion or sterilization. So what I don't understand is if we say that, for example,
sterilization and contraception are part of obstetric and gynecology, why you would decide
to enter that speciality if it was a requirement of the job to deliver those services, that you
could enter cardiology or pathology or another specialty. So I think it's really a more efficient
way of organising a health system. To make clear at the outset, we expect doctors to be providing
these services in these specialities. And if you don't want to do that, do another specialty.
Can you really legislate for it? Because we're quite happy about conscientious objection when
doctors don't participate in torture, for example, where they don't administer lethal injections in
jurisdictions which have capital punishment. So we're pretty happy with conscientious objection
there. Why are we getting antsy about termination and contraception?
Well, torture is illegal and it's not desired by the patient and it's not in the patient's
interest, nor is capital punishment. Those procedures are not part of medical practice
that's governed by law and medical ethics. The point that I'm making is that we want to have
principles that will decide what's appropriate within medicine, and clearly capital punishment
and torture are not appropriate medical practices. But when it comes to we have a vote, we vote in
favour of euthanasia or abortion or contraception, then at one level the debate is over. Doctors can
still campaign for law reform. There are many practices in medicine that are a part of medical
practices that I think are immoral and result in people's death, such as refusing to take organs
from people who have signed organ donation cards. I think that's immoral and it results in people's
death. But if in the end, people are allowed to, or families are allowed to prevent that,
we have to respect that and try to change things by engaging in political or moral debate.
So you're suggesting legislation?

I think, look, as Sweden and Finland have shown, is you can remove a legal right of conscientious objection and deal with these issues as you deal with all labor law, where there's negotiations between individual doctors and their employer around their own personal values.
Now, if there are a small number of doctors who happen to be objecting to a particular practice and many other doctors who can fulfill that need, that can be accommodated.
But what you rapidly see where it becomes a right is many people exercise that right, and often because it's easier for them not to be involved in the performance of those sorts of procedures.
And I think that's at the end of the day, it's the patient that suffers in favour of the doctor's clean conscience.
Given that getting legislation through in the Australian environment is unlikely, what would be the role of medical boards in this, do you believe?
Well, I think medical boards and indeed medical schools should be encouraging doctors to take a 21st century view of the doctor-patient relationship,
where the patient is first and their own personal values are second.
They can engage in discussion with the patient about the options and perhaps even their moral validity,
but in the end, they ought to be there serving the patient and providing a service.
So if indeed we have a right of conscientious objection,
we ought to be encouraging doctors only to exercise that right
in the most extreme of circumstances.
Julian, thanks for joining us.
My pleasure.
Julian Savalesko, who is Professor of Practical Ethics
at the University of Oxford.
I'm Norman Swan, and you've been listening to The Health Report
here on RN, ABC News Radio, and CBC Radio in Canada.
Look forward to your company next week.

simply search for ABC RN.
